name: Liberal democracy
summary: Liberal democracy is a form of government that joins popular rule through free, competitive elections with liberal constitutionalism: rulers hold power by the consent of the governed but are constitutionally bound to respect individual and minority rights. Its defining accounts name universal suffrage, secret ballots and freedom to form parties; guarantees of speech, press, conscience, religion, assembly and property; equality before the law; and separated powers, an independent judiciary and the rule of law that limit what majorities and executives may do. It rests on claims of human equality and universal natural rights going back to Locke, and its adherents divide, as liberal right and liberal left, over how far the state should act in the economy.
scope: Liberal democracy as its defining reference and scholarly accounts set it out: the Gale encyclopedia entry (Watson), Fareed Zakaria's 'The Rise of Illiberal Democracy', Marc Plattner's Journal of Democracy essays, the introduction to Fukuyama's The End of History and the Last Man, and the V-Dem codebook's definition of the liberal democracy index, with Madison's Federalist No. 10, which Plattner names as its vision. It covers the regime type and the principles those sources make part of it, not the policies of particular liberal democratic governments or parties, nor classical liberalism, constitutional liberalism or pluralist democracy as separate ideologies. Policy questions the sources leave open are null; where Gale records the liberal right and liberal left dividing, the answer is a split.

notes: Later pass under rules 5 (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-10). The first pass rested on Wikipedia (s1, s5), on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (s3), which no defining source makes liberal democracy's own text, and on the SEP entry on democracy (s2), which never names liberal democracy; it also recorded many policy questions as 0. Those answers are nulled, each with its reviewHistory, and only positions the defining accounts state are kept. Liberal democracy defines a regime type, so its sources are silent on most economic, social, ecological, technological and foreign-policy statements; the Gale entry records the liberal right and liberal left dividing on state action in the economy, answered as splits only where the statement is about that division. Liberal democracy is the constitutional order of many states, but none makes it a ruling party's doctrine in the sense of PROMPT.md section 3, so no state's record is used and every source is words. Themes searched: government and elections (Gale, Zakaria, Plattner, V-Dem electoral and liberal components, Federalist No. 10), liberty and civil rights (V-Dem civil liberty indicators), religion (V-Dem freedom of religion, Zakaria), economy (Fukuyama, Gale, Zakaria), world (Zakaria and Fukuyama on the liberal peace; Plattner's 'Globalization and Self-Government' was read but states Plattner's own argument, not tenets of liberal democracy, so it is not cited). Not reachable: Merkel's 'Embedded and Defective Democracies' (EconStor returned a bot check), Fukuyama's 1989 essay (the DTIC copy returned 403; other copies are third-party uploads), Diamond's Kellogg working papers (404) and his 1996 Journal of Democracy essay (Project MUSE paywall). Militant democracy and party bans were searched for in the defining sources and not found, so ban-extremist-parties is null.
